strengths: The paper addresses an important and challenging problem: synthesizing an egocentric view from a single exocentric image, with potential relevance to AR/VR, robotics, and instructional content.
EgoWorld combines complementary geometric and semantic cues—depth-derived point clouds, 3D hand poses, and VLM-generated descriptions—in a coherent two-stage framework.
The generated examples are visually promising, particularly for backgrounds and coarse hand-object structure, and substantially improve over the selected baselines under the reported protocol.
The conditioning ablation supports the usefulness of pose and text, while the appendix usefully includes stochastic-generation examples, incorrect-text tests, and failure cases.
The method is computationally accessible, with training reported on a single RTX 4090, and the paper clearly acknowledges dependencies on pose, depth, and language estimators.
weaknesses: The central quantitative evaluation does not test the claimed end-to-end, single-RGB-input system. On H2O, the main experiments use sparse egocentric maps constructed from ground-truth exocentric depth and ground-truth relative camera poses; on TACO, they additionally use ground-truth egocentric hand poses. These are precisely the difficult quantities the proposed observation stage is meant to infer, and the sparse maps visibly reveal substantial target-view appearance. Consequently, the headline results mainly evaluate privileged-input conditional inpainting rather than exocentric-to-egocentric translation.

No quantitative comparison is provided for the complete predicted-input pipeline. The only full-pipeline evidence appears to be a small, unlabeled qualitative real-world study, which cannot establish fidelity because no target egocentric ground truth or user evaluation is available. Thus, claims of state-of-the-art end-to-end performance and strong in-the-wild generalization are not supported.

The proposed egocentric 3D hand-pose estimator—critical for defining the target camera transformation—is evaluated only qualitatively. There are no pose errors, transformation errors, sparse-map quality measurements, robustness tests, or oracle-versus-predicted-input ablations to quantify error propagation.

Baseline selection and comparison are weak. The main baselines are generic image translation, NeRF, and pose-guided person synthesis methods rather than the closest exocentric-to-egocentric methods discussed in related work, such as Exo2Ego and 4Diff. It is also unclear whether baselines receive information comparable in strength to EgoWorld's ground-truth-derived sparse maps and poses.

The experimental splits are insufficiently justified. In particular, the 'unseen actions' split uses the first 80% and last 20% of frames, which may contain near-duplicate temporally adjacent frames and is not necessarily action-disjoint. The unseen-subject setting uses only one training and one testing subject, making broad generalization claims unreliable. Sample counts and repeated-run variability are not reported.

TACO is presented only qualitatively despite being described as a benchmark evaluation, and there is no cross-dataset experiment in which a model trained on one dataset is quantitatively tested on the other.

The formulation leaves important deployment assumptions unclear, including how the desired egocentric camera intrinsics and coordinate frame are chosen from an arbitrary single exocentric photograph. Inferring a unique first-person viewpoint is fundamentally ambiguous when the head or target camera pose is unavailable, as the paper itself notes for TACO.

The reconstruction metrics are limited for a multimodal, under-constrained generation task. PSNR and SSIM against one target penalize plausible alternatives, FID methodology and sample size are unspecified, and there is no human study or task-specific evaluation of hand pose, object identity, contact, or action consistency.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the exact LDM checkpoint and sampling configuration, CFG scale, number of denoising steps, dataset sizes, preprocessing, prompting/model configuration for the VLM, estimator checkpoint details, and baseline training protocols are not sufficiently specified; no code or model-release statement is provided.

The novelty is moderate: the reconstruction network largely combines established latent-diffusion conditioning with projected geometry, pose, and text. The most distinctive component is the observation pipeline, but it is exactly the component bypassed by privileged ground truth in the main evaluation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and challenging problem with potential applications in AR, robotics, and instructional content.
The combination of geometric projection, hand-pose conditioning, textual guidance, and diffusion inpainting is intuitive, and the components provide complementary information.
On H2O, the reconstruction module reports sizable improvements over the evaluated baselines across FID, PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS.
The pose/text conditioning and reconstruction-backbone ablations are useful, and the appendix includes qualitative failure cases and generation-consistency examples.
The manuscript is generally well organized and visually clear, and it provides basic training and compute details.
weaknesses: The principal experiments do not evaluate the claimed single-image, complete pipeline. H2O experiments use ground-truth egocentric sparse maps derived from ground-truth depth and relative camera poses, while TACO additionally uses ground-truth hand poses. These oracle inputs bypass the most difficult observation and camera-transformation stages, so the reported numbers cannot substantiate the central end-to-end or generalization claims.

The closest task-specific methods cited in the paper, particularly Exo2Ego and 4Diff, are omitted from the comparisons. Instead, the quantitative baselines are generic image translation, novel-view synthesis, or pose-guided generation methods. Their inputs also appear weaker than EgoWorld's oracle sparse-map, pose, and text conditions, making the state-of-the-art claim unconvincing.

Novelty is limited: the method primarily combines off-the-shelf depth, hand reconstruction, VLM captioning, Umeyama alignment, and a conventional conditional latent diffusion model. The paper does not establish a substantial new learning or geometric principle beyond this integration.

Important inference assumptions are unresolved. The method requires egocentric camera intrinsics and estimates the exocentric-to-egocentric transform through a learned egocentric 3D hand pose, but it does not explain how the target egocentric camera calibration is obtained for arbitrary real-world inputs. This is especially unclear when no actual egocentric camera exists.

The proposed egocentric hand-pose estimator is evaluated only qualitatively, with no numerical pose or camera-transform errors, robustness analysis, or propagation study. The authors explicitly cannot apply it on TACO, exposing a major limitation of the proposed pipeline.

Evidence beyond H2O is very weak. TACO has no quantitative results and relies on oracle annotations; the in-the-wild study contains only a few selected qualitative examples without ground truth, human evaluation, or semantic-consistency measurements.

The evaluation protocol lacks dataset sizes, exact frame sampling, baseline training details, uncertainty across runs, and a sufficiently precise FID protocol. Defining unseen actions as the last 20% of frames rather than held-out action classes can also create near-duplicate temporal train/test content and does not convincingly measure action generalization.

The metrics emphasize image-level similarity but do not assess the central claims about hand articulation, object identity, interaction correctness, or geometric alignment. For an inherently ambiguous one-to-many prediction problem, PSNR and SSIM against one target are also of limited interpretability.

The text-guidance experiment shows that an incorrect caption can override visual evidence and change object identity. This demonstrates hallucination sensitivity rather than reliable reconstruction, yet the paper interprets it positively and provides no mitigation or quantitative VLM-error analysis.

Calling the system end-to-end is misleading because its modules are separately estimated or frozen, and the primary benchmark ablations concern only the reconstruction stage under privileged inputs. Overall, the empirical support is insufficient for the paper's strongest claims.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and difficult problem with clear relevance to egocentric vision, AR/VR, robotics, and instructional content.
The proposed combination of geometric projection, 3D hand-pose conditioning, textual guidance, and diffusion-based completion is intuitive and practically motivated.
On H2O, the reconstruction module substantially outperforms the evaluated baselines across FID, PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS in all four reported settings.
The conditioning ablation supports the complementary value of pose and text, while the backbone comparison supports the choice of latent diffusion over MAE and MAT variants.

The paper includes useful qualitative analyses covering real-world inputs, repeated generations, incorrect textual guidance, and failure cases. The presentation and visual results are generally clear.
weaknesses: The principal benchmark evaluation does not test the claimed end-to-end single-image method. On H2O, the model receives sparse maps derived from ground-truth depth and ground-truth relative camera poses; on TACO, it receives both ground-truth sparse maps and ground-truth hand poses. These are precisely the quantities the proposed observation stage is meant to infer, so the headline results primarily validate a privileged-input reconstruction model rather than EgoWorld as formulated.

The paper repeatedly claims end-to-end operation and removal of camera-pose assumptions, but provides no quantitative end-to-end benchmark results using predicted depth, poses, intrinsics, transformations, and VLM descriptions. The few unlabeled real-world examples are insufficient to establish accuracy or robustness.

The closest task-specific methods discussed in related work, including Exo2Ego and 4Diff, are absent from the experiments. Comparisons are instead dominated by generic or mismatched baselines such as pix2pixHD, pixelNeRF, and pose-guided person synthesis, weakening the state-of-the-art claim.

The newly introduced egocentric 3D hand-pose estimator receives only qualitative evaluation. There are no pose errors, transformation errors, oracle-versus-predicted-input ablations, or sensitivity analyses showing how depth, pose, calibration, and caption errors affect final output quality.

The experimental protocol is underspecified and potentially misleading. In particular, the purported unseen-actions split is described as training on the first 80% of frames and testing on the last 20%, which does not by itself ensure unseen actions and may permit severe temporal or sequence leakage. Dataset sizes, exact sequence-level splits, FID sample counts, random seeds, and uncertainty are not reported.

TACO results are qualitative only despite being presented as evidence of broad generalization. The in-the-wild study is also small, selectively qualitative, and has neither ground truth nor human evaluation.

Novelty is moderate: most components are established off-the-shelf estimators, Umeyama alignment, and latent-diffusion conditioning. The main contribution is their integration, making rigorous validation of the complete pipeline especially important.

Reproducibility is limited by missing details about preprocessing, sparse-map construction, masking, sampling settings, training data counts, VLM prompting/decoding, and baseline adaptation. No code or trained-model release is stated.

The method assumes a predictable relationship between exocentric appearance and egocentric camera/hand coordinates. This dependence is dataset-specific and becomes infeasible on TACO, as acknowledged by the authors, substantially limiting the claimed generality.
Privacy risks are mentioned, but the proposed safeguards remain generic and are not incorporated into the method or evaluation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and difficult problem with potential relevance to AR/VR, instructional content, and robotics.

EgoWorld combines geometric reprojection, cross-view 3D hand-pose prediction, textual conditioning, and diffusion-based completion in a coherent pipeline. The predicted egocentric hand pose is a useful idea for avoiding an explicitly supplied relative camera pose.

The evaluation covers four datasets, several perceptual and structural metrics, qualitative comparisons, component ablations, noisy inputs, alternative completion backbones, and documented failure cases.
The reported outputs are generally more coherent than those of the implemented baselines, especially for backgrounds and object appearance.
weaknesses: The main evaluation appears to use privileged ground-truth information. On H2O unseen actions, the headline EgoWorld result in Table 1 (e.g., FID 33.284) exactly matches the Table F configuration using ground-truth pose and ground-truth depth. The actual all-predicted pipeline obtains FID 42.323 and substantially worse values on every metric. This directly undermines the claim that the reported state-of-the-art results come from a single RGB image without additional inputs. It is also unclear which configurations produced the headline results on the other datasets.

The baseline comparison is not sufficient to establish state of the art. The most directly related methods, Exo2Ego and 4Diff, are not evaluated; an ablation of EgoWorld is presented as a simulation of 4Diff, which is not an implementation of that method. The remaining baselines largely target different problems, and CFLD receives ground-truth hand layouts, making the comparison difficult to interpret rather than necessarily an upper bound for Exo2Ego.

The generalization protocols are inadequately specified and potentially leaky. In particular, splitting the first 80% and last 20% of temporally adjacent H2O frames does not by itself constitute an unseen-action split. The paper omits dataset-specific training/test counts, frame sampling, synchronization details, and precise protocols for TACO, Assembly101, and Ego-Exo4D.

Several evaluation choices are unclear or potentially circular. The text used for CLIPScore is not specified; if it is the same VLM-generated description used to condition the model, the metric rewards agreement with the model's own input. FID sample counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, and statistical variation are absent, while the consistency analysis contains only a few qualitative samples.

The method is described as end-to-end, but it is a staged composition of separately trained and frozen estimators. Important inference assumptions are also unresolved, including how egocentric camera intrinsics are obtained for an unseen target view. Reproducibility is further limited by the missing project URL, lack of code or trained models, incomplete preprocessing details, and insufficient specification of baseline adaptations.

The real-world evidence is only a small qualitative comparison, with no paired ground truth or quantitative/user evaluation. The failure cases show substantial errors in precisely the fine-grained hand and object geometry motivating the work, limiting support for the stated practical applicability to manipulation-oriented robotics.

strengths: The paper targets an important and challenging problem: synthesizing egocentric observations from a single exocentric image.
Combining projected RGB-D geometry, predicted 3D hand pose, textual context, and diffusion-based completion is intuitively reasonable.
The manuscript includes experiments on four datasets, multiple evaluation metrics, qualitative results, and several component analyses.
weaknesses: The headline evaluation contains a fundamental inconsistency. For H2O unseen actions, Table 1 reports 33.284 FID and 31.620 PSNR as EgoWorld's result. In Table F, these exact numbers correspond to using ground-truth pose and ground-truth depth; the actual all-predicted pipeline obtains 42.323 FID and 28.897 PSNR. Table H again uses the oracle 33.284 result as the default method. Thus, a central claimed result appears to be mislabeled and relies on information unavailable under the stated single-image inference setting. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/036231608b74447e9b771831328f6ef3/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The claimed state-of-the-art comparison is not convincing. The evaluation excludes the most relevant direct methods, Exo2Ego and 4Diff, because their code is unavailable. An ablation of EgoWorld is not a valid simulation of 4Diff, while pix2pixHD, pixelNeRF, and pose-guided CFLD are indirect and often poorly matched baselines.

The H2O 'unseen actions' protocol trains on the first 80% of frames and tests on the last 20%. This does not establish unseen-action generalization and may introduce severe temporal leakage through nearby frames from the same sequences. Split definitions for the other datasets are insufficiently specified.

The claimed single-RGB inference setup is incomplete: the method requires egocentric camera intrinsics, but the paper does not explain how these are obtained for a new in-the-wild image. It also trains a separate exocentric-to-egocentric 3D hand-pose regressor using paired supervision, making the 'end-to-end' characterization misleading.

Evaluation of an inherently ambiguous generation task relies heavily on similarity to one ground-truth frame. There is no human evaluation of realism or interaction correctness, no uncertainty or diversity analysis, no statistical variability, and no reported sample counts for FID. The small, selectively presented in-the-wild comparison is qualitative only.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the project-page URL is blank, and important details such as exact split identifiers, dataset sizes, preprocessing, per-dataset training protocol, diffusion sampler and step count, guidance scale, seeds, VLM decoding configuration, and test-time camera assumptions are missing.

The method hallucinates occluded hands and objects, yet the paper suggests instructional and robotic applications without discussing safety risks from geometrically plausible but incorrect generations. The displayed failure cases confirm that such errors affect precisely the interaction details important to those applications.

Because the central SOTA and generalization claims rest on an apparently oracle-assisted, mislabeled main result and weak protocols, the submission's evaluation is not presently valid enough for acceptance despite the plausible underlying idea.

strengths: The problem—single-image exocentric-to-egocentric view translation—is important for robotics, AR/VR, and instructional applications.
The framework sensibly combines complementary geometric, pose, and semantic cues with diffusion-based completion.
Experiments span four datasets and report diverse perceptual, structural, semantic, and hand-pose metrics.
The appendix includes useful component, conditioning, robustness, completion-backbone, and pose-representation analyses, while the qualitative examples show visually plausible outputs.
weaknesses: The central state-of-the-art claim is undermined by a major evaluation inconsistency. The headline H2O unseen-actions result in Table 1 (FID 33.284, PSNR 31.620) exactly matches Table F's configuration using ground-truth pose and ground-truth depth. The fully predicted pipeline—the setting consistent with the claimed single-RGB-input method—obtains substantially weaker results (FID 42.323, PSNR 28.897). The main table does not disclose these ground-truth inputs, and analogous headline results on the other datasets are not clarified. Thus the advertised end-to-end comparison is unsupported.

The strongest directly relevant prior methods are not actually evaluated. Exo2Ego is replaced by CFLD, and 4Diff is represented by removing conditions from the authors' own architecture. Neither proxy establishes superiority over the corresponding published method; calling the comparisons state of the art is consequently too strong.

Several baselines are poorly matched to the task, including pixelNeRF and pix2pixHD, making large improvements over them relatively uninformative. Fairness is further obscured by differences in input supervision and by insufficient details about baseline adaptation and training.

The purported unseen-action split trains on the first 80% of frames and tests on the last 20%, which can retain the same videos, actions, environments, and temporally adjacent content. This is not convincing evidence of generalization to unseen action classes. Other splits are also very small—for example, one training and one test subject—and dataset sizes and overlap controls are not reported.

The single-image inference claim is incomplete because the method requires egocentric camera intrinsics, but the manuscript does not explain how these are obtained at inference. Exocentric intrinsics are said to come from the depth estimator, whereas the source of egocentric intrinsics remains unspecified.

The method is an incremental integration of off-the-shelf depth, hand reconstruction, VLM captioning, rigid alignment, and latent-diffusion inpainting. Its value could still be meaningful, but the current experiments do not isolate novelty from stronger pretrained components or compare under matched inputs.

Reproducibility is limited: the project URL is blank, code is unavailable, exact checkpoints and sampling settings are missing, dataset sample counts are absent, and important details about preprocessing, camera calibration, baseline tuning, and FID computation are unspecified.

The in-the-wild evidence is only a small qualitative comparison without ground truth, user evaluation, or quantitative geometric validation. It cannot substantiate the claimed practical applicability or robustness.

Failure cases acknowledge errors from occlusion, subtle finger motion, and VLM hallucination, but uncertainty, safety implications for manipulation, and sensitivity to erroneous upstream estimates are not rigorously characterized; the manually selected noisy subset is not reproducible.
